entities.summary:
The 1918–1920 flu pandemic was a devastating global outbreak of the H1N1 influenza A virus, which claimed the lives of an estimated 50 million people, roughly 3-5% of the world's population. The pandemic occurred during the final year of World War I and spread rapidly across the globe, infecting millions and overwhelming healthcare systems. It is considered one of the deadliest natural disasters in human history, with its impact still felt today in the development of modern medicine and public health policies.

The pandemic began in March 1918 in the city of Kansas, USA, and quickly spread to other parts of the world, including Europe and Asia. The virus was particularly deadly among young adults, who were more susceptible to its effects due to the lack of immunity in the population. As the pandemic spread, cities and towns were forced to implement quarantine measures, mask mandates, and other public health policies to try and contain the outbreak.

The 1918-1920 flu pandemic had a profound impact on the world, leading to significant changes in the way that governments and healthcare systems respond to public health crises. It also led to major advances in the development of vaccines and other medical treatments, which have saved countless lives in the decades since.

The pandemic's impact can still be felt today, as the world continues to grapple with the challenges of infectious disease and the need for global cooperation in responding to public health crises.

With an estimated 50 million deaths and 500 million cases, the 1918-1920 flu pandemic was a defining moment in human history, a reminder of the power of nature and the importance of human resilience and determination in the face of adversity.
